title: State, private groups settle suit with St. Mary’s utility over sewage spills
summary: State and environmental officials reached a partial settlement with the utility that provides water and sewer services to St. Mary's County to upgrade facilities blamed for discharges of raw sewage into the Potomac River and its tributaries.
content:
by Maryland Matters Staff, Maryland Matters August 5, 2024

by Maryland Matters Staff, Maryland Matters August 5, 2024

State and environmental officials said they have reached a partial settlement with the utility that provides water and sewer services to St. Mary’s County to upgrade facilities that were blamed for discharges of raw sewage into the Potomac River and its tributaries.

The suit was filed in late 2022 by the Maryland Department of the Environment, the Potomac Riverkeeper Network and Shore Thing Shellfish against the St. Mary’s Metropolitan Commission, the quasi-governmental nonprofit that provides water and sewer services to St. Mary’s County.

It claimed that the utility was allowing discharges of raw sewage from its facilities into the county’s waterways.

The settlement noted that the commission has already taken some action to correct problems and it has more work planned. MetCom said in a later statement that the consent decree was referring to what it identified as more than $37 million in projects that were under way, were already funded or were approved as part of its capital improvement program.

But the state also noted in court documents that while the lawsuit was pending, the utility allowed more than 76,000 gallons of sewage spills between Dec. 15, 2022, and June 10, 2024. The state also claimed the utility exceeded discharge limits for phosphorous and nitrogen in late 2022.

The 78-page settlement calls on the commission to begin immediate repairs and upgrades to pump stations that have been the main culprits in the spills , to develop new models for system testing and to conduct comprehensive evaluations of its entire system for at least the next nine years.

The consent decree also requires that the utility develop an emergency response plan and reporting protocols for any future spills.

The agreement includes a $250,500 penalty to be paid by St. Mary’s MetCom: Half of that amount will go to the Department of the Environment and the other half will be directed to the Potomac River Fisheries Commission to help fund oyster restoration projects “that have a reasonable nexus to water quality impacts associated with the violations that are the subject of this Consent Decree.”

MetCom Director George Erichsen said in a staement that the agency was “pleased to have been able to work with Potomac River Fisheries Commission on the scope and funding of a supplemental environmental project for oyster revitalization in the lower Potomac River that was eventually included in the decree.”

Erichsen called the decree the product of “lengthy and cooperative discussions” between the parties, and said actions that will be required under the agreement “should be useful tools in helping to inform future rehabilitation priorities” and to “enhance documents and processes already in place.”

Officials with the state and the private groups welcomed the agreement.

“This settlement is about accountability and clean water progress,” said Jay Apperson, a Department of the Environment spokesperson. “It includes a significant financial penalty, half of which will go toward an important environmental project. It also establishes a comprehensive framework to address sewer overflows.”

Potomac Riverkeeper Network President Nancy Stoner said the action will force MetCom to “take immediate steps to halt sewage overflows and to undertake a comprehensive plan for upgrading its whole system to ensure they do not recur. The result is a win for the river, the oysters, watermen, and the public.”

– This story was updated on Tuesday, Aug. 6, to include comment from the St. Mary’s Metropolitan Commission.
